title: Customer Health Score Automation: 2026 Setup Guide
summary: Customer health score automation tools differ by data location and scoring maintenance. Find the right tool for your infrastructure and maintenance model.
body_markdown:
## ChurnZero for prepared CS teams


If you run a mid-size CS team that already sends clean product usage into ChurnZero and has people ready to act on health scores, it suits you. For anyone else it's the wrong buy as of 24 November 2026.


ChurnZero tracks usage in real time and rolls events into health scores you configure. It fires automated plays (a task, an email, an alert to the account owner) when a score moves.


The case for watching usage at all is cost.[CloudRatings](https://research.cloudratings.com/view/331889279) puts the CAC ratio for a new logo at 1.78 to 2 dollars, against 0.61 to 1 dollar for expansion.


Winning a stranger costs roughly twice what growing an existing customer does, and expansion runs at about a third to a half of the acquisition price. A score that catches a slipping account early protects the cheaper revenue.


### Gainsight setup and ongoing maintenance effort


Expect the effort to sit in scoring. You decide which usage events count and how much each weighs, so the score is only as good as the events feeding it.


If your product emits patchy events, you pay a platform licence to score noise. Other data, such as CRM and support records, arrives as feeds someone must keep working.


Price it the way you'd price a retainer. The licence is one line, but the person who tunes the scores and runs the plays is usually the larger one.


Across a whole book of business, the accounts that generate clear signals end up carrying the cost of those that generate none.


Compare that with a general automation tool's project settings, shown below. The only capacity control on the General tab is Max Concurrent Jobs, left at Default (5), which caps the project at five flows running at the same time.


Because a nightly scoring run is one flow, five at once leaves room for the rest of the project's automations. At that scale, capacity is a number you read off a settings page, not a contract you negotiate.


Where ChurnZero stops short is the data and people you must bring. It's the wrong buy in three cases:


1. Your usage data lives in spreadsheets or an export you assemble by hand, not in events sent continuously from the product.
2. No one owns the scores weekly, so plays fire into an inbox nobody works.
3. Your CS team is small enough that a scored list in a shared sheet, refreshed on a schedule, would already cover every account it can personally call.


In any of those, buying the platform first means paying for scoring you can't yet feed or act on.


For that third case, Activepieces runs a weekly scoring workflow over your CRM, billing and support apps, any of its 750+ integrations. It is not a customer success platform and has no built-in health dashboard, so the weights are yours to own.


The first version doesn't need a builder, though. Describe the weekly scoring process in the built-in chat, naming those three apps, and what comes back is a published flow in your account, the same kind of artifact someone would otherwise wire by hand.


It sits under the same RBAC and audit logs as every other flow, and each execution leaves a run trace you can open and read. MoneyGram and Moneypenny run Activepieces in production.
